questions.prompt: Leila's language examination comes in two halves. In June she answers on paper, alone at a desk, for three hours. In July she sits facing two teachers and answers out loud. What are the two halves, in the order she takes them?

options.text: the practical first, then the theoretical
the oral paper first, then the written
the written paper first, then the oral
the theoretical first, then the practical

questions.explanation: Answering on paper is the written part; answering out loud, facing the person who will mark you, is the oral. June comes before July, so that is the order, and the reverse order describes a different candidate's year. The other pair answers a different question altogether: practical and theoretical separate what is done with your hands in a laboratory from what is known and stays on the page, which is why a science examination has both and a language examination has neither.

questions.prompt: Sami hands in an essay written as one solid block: every line runs from the very edge of the sheet on the left to the very edge on the right, and nothing breaks the text from the first line to the last. His teacher asks for two changes in the next one. Which two?

options.text: a margin down the side, and a new paragraph at each new idea
a margin down the side, and a full stop after each new idea
a new chapter at each new idea, and a wider space between the lines
a full stop at the foot of the page, and a title above each part

questions.explanation: Two things are missing from that sheet, and each has its own name. The strip left blank along the side is the margin: it exists so that a teacher can write there, and an essay written edge to edge leaves nobody any room. And a text is cut into paragraphs, one for each idea, which is what makes an argument readable. A full stop cannot do that work, because it closes a sentence and an idea normally takes several; chapters cut up a book, never a three-page essay.

questions.prompt: A notice goes up on the board: "The hall is too small for the whole year group to sit the mock examination together." What is the head teacher telling the pupils?

options.text: the hall is small, but the year group will just fit into it
the hall is small, and so the examination has been called off
the year group will sit the paper in the hall, as it always does
the whole year group cannot sit the paper together in that hall

questions.explanation: This structure carries its own negative: once a quality has passed the point where an action remains possible, the action does not take place, and no not has to be written. That is the whole difference with very, which only measures the room and leaves everyone free to squeeze in. Notice also how little the notice rules out — one arrangement, in one room. It cancels no examination; and reading it as business as usual simply ignores the word the whole sentence turns on.

questions.prompt: Every morning the school office notes which pupils are present and which are missing, and sends the totals to the ministry at the end of the term. What is the office keeping a record of?

options.text: attention
attendance
attending
attendant

questions.explanation: One verb, one ending, one noun: attend takes -ance and gives the name of exactly what those registers hold, the fact of being there. Attention is a different thing entirely — what a pupil gives the lesson once he is sitting in it — and no register has ever been able to count it. An attendant is a person, somebody whose job is to look after a place. And the -ing form is still the verb at work, where the sentence has left a hole that only a noun can fill.

questions.prompt: A full page in a magazine shows a photograph of children eating at school. Below the last line of text, two lines are printed and nothing else: a web address of the form www.…org, and an e-mail address beginning with fundraising@. What do those two lines alone tell a reader?

options.text: the page was placed by a company that is advertising its food
the page was placed by a school that is looking for new pupils
the page was placed by an organisation that is asking for gifts
the page was placed by a newspaper that is selling its magazine

questions.explanation: The tail of a web address says what kind of body owns it, and .org is worn by organisations rather than by shops. The first word of an e-mail address names the desk you would be writing to, and one that opens on fundraising announces people whose whole job is collecting money. So the two lines that almost no reader looks at have quietly named the sender and its purpose. A firm selling food, a school hunting for pupils or a magazine selling itself would each have printed something else there: a shop address, a price, a subscription form.
